Research report · 10 October 2026

Notebook investigations for explorEDA

11 inspected examples • 7 Observable notebooks • 4 computational essays and investigations

The best references build an argument one result at a time: a question leads to a calculation, its output changes the next question, and the reader can inspect the steps. The selected examples cover simple summaries, grouped comparisons, time series, missing-data sensitivity, model evaluation and spatial statistics. Each example begins with captured evidence of the actual page.

Recommended first reproductions
  • Small first proof: What's different? Timeseries forecast performance
  • Broader representative workflow: Discovering Date Patterns
  • Stretch case: Is Seattle Really Seeing an Uptick In Cycling?

Selection and evidence

  • Seven of the eleven selections are Observable notebooks. Eleven is deliberate: quality and inspectability took priority over adding a twelfth marginal example.
  • Four Observable selections share an electricity-analysis collection but exercise different patterns: subtraction, decomposition, calendar features and joins/conditional comparisons. The two penguin examples likewise show a progression from grouped exploration to model-informed revision.
  • The main reading sequence matters in every selection. Some individual outputs contain facets, adjacent maps or a chart/table switch. Reproducing the essay does not require arranging unrelated charts in a dashboard grid.
  • No example requires elaborate animation for its analytical core. Maps, resampling and model fitting remain meaningful capability questions, not assumed features of explorEDA.

How to read the evidence

  • Actual analysis pages were opened and inspected in their rendered state. Screenshots are captures of those pages, not gallery thumbnails or generated mockups. Some captures show a revealed solution, changed control, or later analytical step; captions identify those states.
  • Observable source was inspected through visible cells and, where useful, archived exports of the author's notebook source checked against the live page. An archived revision is identified when used. Search snippets alone were not treated as evidence.
  • Observable's visible JavaScript was inspected as evidence of source methods. Equivalent expressions, queries and chart configurations may reproduce those methods; these references do not imply that explorEDA needs a general JavaScript runtime.
  • Data availability distinguishes a working live attachment/table, an inspected downloadable snapshot, and an upstream source that was linked but not independently retrieved. Exact formulas are described only when supported by visible source or documented methods.
  • Observed controls are labeled separately from proposed explorEDA controls. Every compatibility statement is a hypothesis based on the supplied capabilities; explorEDA itself was not inspected. Effort ratings are relative scope judgments, not schedules.
  • Two retained notebooks have localized execution failures: Bratenahl's sensitivity output and two spatial-tutorial cells. Their functioning analytical sequences and visible methods remain useful; the failures and reproduction limits are specified in their entries.

Screened out

  • The Olympics age-by-sport companion notebook currently displayed errors instead of its plots, so it was excluded.
  • An AWS EC2 pricing investigation had a missing CSV attachment and failed chart outputs. It was excluded despite a promising narrative.
  • A Taylor Swift Plot workshop had working visual controls but limited investigative argument and failing SQL outputs. It was screened out of the main set.
  • Data releases, single-chart examples and generic platform demos were not added merely to fill the target count.

Observable · Raw observations → grouped comparison → faceted distributions → summary overlay

What the analysis does

The notebook investigates how penguin body measurements vary by species, sex and island. A raw mass-versus-flipper relationship becomes more informative when species color and then sex facets are added; later questions compare counts, weight distributions and medians. In the inspected charts, longer flippers tend to accompany greater mass, and the groups separate differently across the comparisons. That is our visual interpretation. The author supplies questions and executable solutions rather than a concluding biological claim. This is a guided investigation using real research data, so it is strongest as a small, progressive reproduction, with the pedagogical character stated explicitly.

Role of prose. Each question gives the preceding result a reason to change: first relate two measurements, then distinguish species without discarding the relationship, then add sex without losing the species encoding. Later prose motivates counting, binning and median overlays. Hints explain the calculation or encoding; interpretation is largely left to the reader. The notebook therefore demonstrates a sequence of analytical decisions more strongly than a finished computational essay.

Source data and calculations

Original source. Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research; the Palmer Penguins dataset distributed by Allison Horst and colleagues, with a notebook-specific CSV attachment.

Row grain and scope. One measured penguin; 344 records spanning Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins on Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Canonical provenance covers 2007–2009; the notebook attachment omits year.

Fields and units. species, island, bill_length, bill_depth, flipper_length, body_mass and sex. Lengths are millimeters; mass is grams. The attachment uses MALE/FEMALE and blank sex values, and removes unit suffixes from column names. The canonical CSV retains year, _mm/_g suffixes and lowercase sex values.

  • Exact attached palmer-penguins.csv
  • Original dataset documentation and attribution
  • Canonical CSV source file
  • Canonical CSV direct download
  • Original study

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • The attachment loads with typed CSV parsing. No explicit row-cleaning step precedes the inspected comparisons. Missing measurements and sex need an explicit policy in a reproduction; the sex-faceted solution visibly retains a blank category.
  • Questions 1–3 use raw observations: x = flipper_length, y = body_mass; Question 2 adds fill and hover title = species; Question 3 keeps those encodings and facets horizontally by sex.
  • Question 4 groups by species and counts records for a bar chart. Question 5 repeats species counts within island facets; an alternative uses x = island, y = species and radius = count.
  • Question 6 bins body_mass and counts rows using Plot.binX with thresholds: 20. Questions 7–8 facet these histograms by sex horizontally and species vertically. The threshold is a requested bin parameter; do not assume it guarantees exactly twenty rendered bins under the library's defaults.
  • Question 8 overlays a full-height median tick on each sex/species distribution using Plot.groupZ({x: 'median'}, {x: 'body_mass'}), within the existing facet context.
  • Question 9 asks how many females exceed the lightest male. Its supplied solution shows male extrema, female median and individual observations by species. It does not produce the requested count, so an exact numerical answer would be an extension rather than an observed output.

What feeds later results. The shared data table feeds every chart. The analytical dependency is progressive—each comparison motivates the next—but the original chart cells generally repeat their definitions rather than consuming the preceding chart's output. Within the statistics chart, the histogram counts and median reducer share the same raw rows and facet groups.

Reproduction sufficiency. The actual attachment link, loaded table and visible solution definitions are sufficient for the core reproduction. Data provenance is public and documented. The canonical CSV is an accessible substitute if the attachment fails: rename columns, normalize sex values and preserve missingness. This changes schema preparation, not the intended sample, but identity with the attachment should be checked before claiming a byte-for-byte match.

Limits and uncertainty. This is a teaching investigation, with fewer authored conclusions than the journalism examples. Native table sorting and row selection are visible, but no source dependency links the table selection to the charts. Hint/Solution toggles change presentation; they are not analytical filters. The exact Question 9 count is absent.

Elements needed to reproduce it

  1. Introduce the measured penguins → load and inspect rows → establish fields and missing values.
  2. Ask whether heavier birds have longer flippers → configure a raw scatter → inspect the association.
  3. Ask whether species explain the pattern → add species color and hover labels → compare clusters.
  4. Ask about sex while retaining species → facet the same scatter by sex → compare within groups.
  5. Ask how sample composition varies → count species, then species within islands → inspect bars or a count table.
  6. Ask about weight distributions → bin mass by sex/species → overlay group medians → inspect overlap and formulate the next question.

Fit for explorEDA

Smallest faithful version. Reproduce Questions 1–3 with the data table: a mass/flipper scatter, a second block adding species color, and a third adding sex facets, joined by the original analytical questions. This is a small first proof. Counts and a histogram-plus-median can extend it when grouped calculations are ready.

Likely fit, subject to verification. Tables, interactive charts, filters, calculated fields and saved state appear sufficient for much of the exploration, based only on the product description. No arbitrary JavaScript execution is implied by these requirements.

Capabilities to investigate. Facets with shared scales, grouped counts and medians, histogram bin defaults, overlay marks, explicit missing-category behavior, and whether copied or derived chart definitions preserve common configuration without coupling every later edit.

Graphical edits that should update text. Visual changes to x/y fields, species color, sex or island facet, category order, opacity, hover fields, axis units, bin thresholds and median overlays should update the defining text. A switch from raw observations to counts must update the calculation as well as the chart encoding. The text should expose the grouping and denominator, not merely record cosmetic changes.

Control scope. The original exposes table inspection and solution toggles, not a shared analytical filter. A proposed global species filter would affect every dependent result; changing one chart's color or facet should remain local unless the text explicitly shares that setting. Histogram and median layers need identical group/filter scope.

Execution and editing lesson. This tests whether users can express a familiar calculation/visual combination in text, refine it with graphical controls, and read a meaningful sequence afterward. It also tests the distinction between a shared dataset, a copied chart definition and a true dependent calculation. Missing values must remain legible when a visual edit introduces a facet.

Observable · Actual versus forecast → signed difference → event-window investigation

What the analysis does

The notebook investigates hourly Texas demand around the February 2021 power crisis. Subtracting the forecast from actual demand makes two dips before the rolling blackouts noticeable. This is a particularly clear example of an analytical argument produced by changing what is calculated and displayed. It does not establish why those early dips occurred; price is offered as a follow-up hypothesis.

Role of prose. The prose introduces an apparent comparison problem, asks whether demand was above or below forecast, explains the signed difference, interprets the pre-event pattern, and motivates a closer date window. The later diagrams explain why comparing two sloping lines can obscure that difference.

Source data and calculations

Original source. U.S. Energy Information Administration Open Data, an ERCOT/Texas hourly demand and day-ahead-forecast snapshot downloaded in August 2021 and attached in September 2021.

Row grain and scope. One hourly observation in Texas/ERCOT, January–February 2021; the live raw and renamed arrays contain 1,417 rows. The fixed event-window subset contains 216 rows.

Fields and units. date (UTC timestamp), demand renamed actuals, and forecast. The chart labels demand in MWh, but some explanatory text uses kW; retain raw values and reconcile this source labeling inconsistency rather than applying an invented conversion.

  • Exact attached Texas demand/forecast CSV
  • EIA original provider
  • Author’s EIA download notebook

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Parse the attached CSV with typed fields; rename demand to actuals.
  • Compute signed difference actuals − forecast; positive and negative values receive consistent orange and purple encodings.
  • Represent rolling blackouts at 2021-02-15T07:25:00Z (1:25 a.m. CST). Filter the zoom from 2021-02-07T07:25:00Z through 2021-02-16T07:25:00Z inclusively.
  • The source derives daily/weekly ticks from UTC intervals shifted six hours to show Central time, and derives maxima for chart/annotation placement (maxDelta 10,436 and maxValue 76,783 in the inspected state).

What feeds later results. Typed data → renamed relation → actual/forecast line charts and residual charts. The zoom predicate produces a smaller relation reused by later line and residual comparisons. Shared event and semantic-color definitions feed multiple graphics and explanatory annotations.

Reproduction sufficiency. The live loaded rows, downloadable attachment link, visible transformation definitions and stated subtraction are enough for the analytical core. The attachment bytes were not independently downloaded. A failed browser download did not prevent the notebook itself from loading and displaying the data.

Limits and uncertainty. Unit labels are inconsistent; do not preserve them uncritically. The event window is a fixed authored filter, not a reader-operated brush. The early demand decline is an observed temporal relationship, not a demonstrated cause. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit.

Elements needed to reproduce it

  1. Introduce the forecast question → inspect hourly actual/forecast values → show two lines and blackout annotation.
  2. Explain the desired comparison → derive actuals minus forecast → show signed differences around zero.
  3. Interpret the unexpected pre-blackout dips → filter to the nine-day event window → show the enlarged residual pattern → propose a follow-up question.

Smallest faithful version. Keep the introduction, original two-line chart, explicit residual calculation, signed-error plot and nine-day zoom with interpretation. The conceptual cartoons and repeated return to the original chart are optional.

Likely fit, subject to verification. Calculated fields, filters, interactive chart definitions, tables and saved analysis state appear to cover the core, based only on the product description.

Capabilities to investigate. Shared named calculations across blocks; positive/negative rule or bar encodings; event and text annotations; a clear distinction between display-domain edits and upstream date filtering; consistent units and semantic colors.

Graphical edits that should update text. Graphical changes to mark type, axis fields and limits, color assignments, event position/label, annotation text and window bounds should update the relevant block text. Changing a residual chart’s visual style should preserve the subtraction it depends on.

Control scope. There are no main reader controls in the inspected notebook. The authored event filter affects the zoomed branch, while the complete series remains available above.

Execution and editing lesson. A small calculation can be the analytical turning point. This tests whether two-way editing preserves a named derived field, reuses it in a later block, and records local view changes without accidentally changing the evidence above.

Observable · Aggregate anomaly → category decomposition → shared-scale comparisons

What the analysis does

A fictional analyst investigates a spike in real Texas generation data. Successive views show a two-week episode, not just one high day: a coal plateau, a nuclear dip, sustained lower wind generation, and a large rise in natural-gas generation. The epilogue explicitly says the aggregate patterns cannot determine which fuel is intrinsically better or worse or by themselves establish the crisis mechanism.

Role of prose. The story gives each chart a reason to exist: confirm the total, identify contributing categories, address overlapping lines, examine stacking, and finally separate fuel types with comparable scales. Interpretation then accompanies each selected fuel panel.

Source data and calculations

Original source. EIA Open Data hourly net generation by fuel for the Texas region; a cached API response deliberately attached so the article remains reproducible.

Row grain and scope. One fuel category × UTC hour in January–February 2021, Texas region. The live transformed array has 9,912 rows, covering seven fuels: coal, natural gas, nuclear, other, solar, hydro and wind.

Fields and units. series_id/id, series name/name, derived type, parsed UTC date, and value. The y-axis divides values by 1,000. Source labels vary between thousand megawatts and thousand megawatt hours per day; the facet code uses hourly rows directly, so a daily-total interpretation is unsupported.

  • Exact attached texasCrisis2021.json
  • EIA original provider
  • EIA grid monitor used for fuel colors

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Load cached JSON; flatten each series’ date/value pairs; extract fuel type from the series name; parse %Y%m%dT%HZ as UTC; sort by date.
  • The total-generation line bins by UTC hour and sums value across fuel records. Its opening variant applies a window with k=1, which does not smooth the data.
  • Later fuel lines and stacked areas map the same date/value rows with type determining grouping and color. Faceting splits by type while retaining a common y scale.
  • Selected-fuel panels highlight the February 7–21 episode. Exact styling/shading helper logic was not fully inspected; the underlying fuel comparison and scale transforms were visible.

What feeds later results. One cleaned long relation feeds the total aggregation, fuel lines, stacked areas, facets and individual fuel views. A shared semantic fuel-color mapping also supports colored phrases in the prose.

Reproduction sufficiency. The cached 215KB JSON link, populated table, visible load/cleaning source, and inspected chart definitions support the core reproduction. Bytes were not independently downloaded. Reproducing the original obsolete EIA API URL is unnecessary because the frozen attachment is present.

Limits and uncertainty. The source’s hourly-versus-daily and power-versus-energy wording should be resolved explicitly. The notebook decomposes measured generation; it is not a causal model of generation failures, unmet demand or fuel reliability. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit.

Elements needed to reproduce it

  1. Receive an anomaly question → acquire detailed hourly fuel data → inspect the records.
  2. Sum fuel categories per hour → reproduce the total line → ask what contributes.
  3. Split lines by fuel → try stacked area → explain why overlap and moving baselines hinder comparison.
  4. Facet with common scales → inspect selected fuels in separate full-width panels → interpret the two-week episode and state causal limits.

Smallest faithful version. Keep the anomaly, source table, hourly total, category lines and fuel facets, followed by the four short findings. An initial reproduction can omit the fictional office framing, stack intermediate and custom highlight styling.

Likely fit, subject to verification. Grouping, aggregation, charts, calculated fields and filters appear compatible with the described capabilities; this remains a hypothesis.

Capabilities to investigate. Common-scale faceting, stable category color mappings shared with prose, named aggregate versus detail relations, and preserving independently authored comparisons while editing chart configurations.

Removing grouping is a calculation/configuration change with analytical consequences and should remain explicit.

Observable · Time series → calendar features → grouped distributions

What the analysis does

The question is how much structure can be discovered from only a timestamp and a measured value. The notebook first smooths California electricity demand, then derives local calendar categories and compares distributions within them. Its reported patterns vary by hour and season; the inspected quarter-by-day view also makes weekday/weekend differences visible. This is an analytical walkthrough with interpretation, rather than a set of unrelated charts.

Role of prose. The prose introduces the restricted starting information, explains why smoothing helps, motivates additional date fields, and uses the first results to choose the next comparison. It also distinguishes UTC display time from local calendar time and closes by explaining how the same reasoning transfers to other timestamp/value data.

Source data and calculations

Original source. U.S. Energy Information Administration Open Data; an attached California-region hourly-demand snapshot used by the notebook.

Row grain and scope. One California-region hourly demand observation; 8,784 rows for the local 2020 leap year. The final local-hour record is stored as 2021-01-01T07:00Z.

Fields and units. date (UTC timestamp) and value (electricity demand, chart-labelled MWh). Derived fields are local hour, day of month, weekday, weekend/weekday, ISO week, month and quarter, using America/Los_Angeles.

  • Exact attached california.csv
  • EIA original provider
  • Author's EIA download notebook
  • Archived authored source, revision 1760

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Parse the timestamp and derive calendar features in America/Los_Angeles, preserving the original instant for the time axis.
  • The rolling transform uses k = 1, 24, 168 or 672 hourly observations. The source delegates alignment and edge handling to its Observable Plot version; those defaults were not independently resolved.
  • The date brush supplies the line's x-domain and masks points outside the interval. It does not filter the data used by the later grouped output.
  • The later chart groups raw observations by the two selected calendar categories. Each group displays demand values as ticks and its mean as the colored background; group means also feed tooltips. Weekday and month orders are explicit.

What feeds later results. raw_data → enriched data → inspected table and grouped distributions. enriched data + smoothing choice + brush limits → line chart. Grouping selectors affect the faceted result and tooltip summaries, while the earlier smoothing and brush controls remain local to the line.

Reproduction sufficiency. The live table, attached CSV link and visible/archived authored transformations are sufficient for the core reproduction. The attachment link was inspected and the notebook loaded its rows; the CSV bytes were not independently downloaded. The archive is a preserved revision and was checked against live behavior, not assumed to be the current page wholesale.

Limits and uncertainty. Resolve window alignment, edge behavior and sort order explicitly for an exact match. The source uses a PST tooltip label throughout the year despite deriving daylight-saving-aware local fields; a faithful analytical reproduction should label the timezone clearly. This is a labeling issue, not evidence of incorrect local feature derivation. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit.

Elements needed to reproduce it

  1. Explain the timestamp-only question → load and inspect date/value rows.
  2. Define a rolling window and visible date extent → show the time series → interpret daily and seasonal structure.
  3. Explain local calendar features → derive them → display the enriched table.
  4. Choose two grouping dimensions → show demand distributions and group means → compare seasonal and weekday patterns.

Smallest faithful version. Use the two-column snapshot, a raw-data table, one rolling line and one quarter-by-weekday grouped chart. Keep the text that motivates the move from time to calendar categories. A mean-by-group chart can be an initial simplification, but it should be labeled as losing the distribution information.

Likely fit, subject to verification. Tables, calculated calendar fields, filters, interactive charts and saved state appear to cover much of this workflow, based only on the supplied product description.

Capabilities to investigate. Timezone-aware date extraction, rolling windows with explicit defaults, two-dimensional facets, per-group distribution marks, and control bindings to a specific result. These are capability questions rather than requirements for arbitrary JavaScript execution.

Graphical edits that should update text. Changing the smoothing window, axis domain, facet fields, category order, tick opacity, mean color scale, labels or tooltip content should update the corresponding block definition. A facet change that changes aggregation should update both grouping and result configuration, rather than only its visual layout.

Control scope. Observed controls have different scopes: smoothing and brush are local to the line; the later selectors recompute only grouped comparisons. A future global date filter would be a different, explicitly declared behavior.

Execution and editing lesson. The reading sequence and calculation dependencies are related but not identical. An enriched table can feed separate branches, each with local control state. Two-way editing should preserve those branches and expose defaults such as window size and calendar timezone in text.

Observable · Time-aligned join → visual relationship → calendar-conditioned comparisons

What the analysis does

The notebook asks how the relationship between Texas electricity demand and temperature changes over time. It moves from a crowded colored scatterplot to calendar facets. Its worked interpretation compares 10 a.m. with other hours: demand is relatively higher at low temperatures and lower at high temperatures. The analysis is visual; the current notebook does not calculate a linear correlation coefficient or regression.

Role of prose. The prose defines the comparison, explains the join’s geographical assumption, diagnoses occlusion and legend effort, motivates spatial separation, and interprets the shapes against the full-data background.

Source data and calculations

Original source. EIA Texas electricity demand and NOAA Dallas/Fort Worth airport weather, downloaded through the authors’ companion notebooks and attached as CSVs.

Row grain and scope. One matched UTC hour from late September 2019 to late September 2021. Live demand contains 17,545 rows; the temperature and joined arrays each contain 17,528. The complete archived weather CSV matching the live attachment hash was inspected, confirming the period.

Fields and units. date; value renamed demand (MWh); air_temp renamed temp (°C); precomputed hour, day, weekend, week, month, quarter, daytime and feel. Demand covers Texas while temperature is from one airport.

  • Exact attached demand CSV
  • Exact attached weather/features CSV
  • NOAA original hourly-weather source
  • Author’s weather download notebook
  • Archived authored source, revision 1969

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Typed-load both CSVs; join on their shared UTC hourly timestamp; rename measured fields and drop series id/name.
  • Color the scatter by a selected time category. Random drawing order and opacity 0.5 reduce the effect of occlusion.
  • The faceted view groups by a separately selected category. A constant-gray binned occupancy layer of the entire dataset is repeated in every facet; source bin widths are 1°C and 1,000 MWh. Colored dots show each subset.
  • Calendar category labels and ordering are explicit; a shared palette feeds both the scatter and facets.

What feeds later results. Joined data feeds the table and both chart branches. One radio controls scatter color grouping; another controls faceting. The palette selector is shared. The gray background deliberately references all joined rows rather than the current facet subset. One finer dependency appears in archived revision 1969: the first scatter category also controls whether the Cividis palette is reversed in the faceted view. That styling dependency was found in source, not tested as a live interaction.

Reproduction sufficiency. The actual controls worked and the join, attachments, schema and preserved source are visible. The archive was checked against the live narrative, data hashes and behavior; it is a pinned revision, not presumed identical to every current UI detail.

Limits and uncertainty. The exact cutoffs of precomputed daytime and feel categories were not verified; use the attached columns or restrict a minimum version to explicit hour/month categories. A statewide demand series and one airport temperature series have different geographic scope, an assumption the notebook itself discusses. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit. The timezone used to create the attached calendar-category columns was not independently established; use the supplied fields for the reference reproduction. Joined row counts alone do not verify one-to-one matching or identify all unmatched-hour cases.

Elements needed to reproduce it

  1. Ask about a changing relationship → load and align hourly sources → display the joined table.
  2. Color temperature-versus-demand by a time category → inspect overlap → try alternate palettes.
  3. Separate calendar categories into facets → repeat the full-data gray reference → compare hourly distributions and interpret the 10 a.m. pattern.

Observable · Missing-data sensitivity → grouped rates → association → geographic corroboration

What the analysis does

The investigation asks whether Bratenahl's traffic enforcement disproportionately affects Black drivers and how incomplete race recording changes that assessment. It first examines missing data, then compares recording and race patterns across officers, and finally checks the neighborhoods where ticketed people live. In the rendered geographic tables, 498 of 956 tract-matched ticket records are associated with majority-Black tracts, and 776 with tracts below the stated Ohio median household income. These describe the matched records, not all stops or traffic exposure. The structure works because each section addresses a limitation or alternative explanation raised by the previous one, with prose interpreting the results and introducing a corroborating lens.

Role of prose. Prose establishes the reporting question, explains why two administrative sources answer different questions, makes missingness a methodological issue, interprets officer-level comparisons, and motivates geographic corroboration. It closes with reporting checks from court observations and sampled arrest records. This is one of the clearest examples of an argument requiring prose and results to remain in order.

Source data and calculations

Original source. Bratenahl police stop records and ticket records obtained by the reporting team, supplemented with geocoded addresses and Census-derived tract attributes. The companion investigation was published by The Marshall Project and Cleveland reporting partners.

Row grain and scope. Stops: 4,048 police stop records, January 1, 2020–September 15, 2022. Tickets: 1,006 ticket records for January 1–September 15, 2022, with geocoded home locations. These are separate sources and grains. No deduplication proving one ticket row equals one unique driver was verified. Scope is Bratenahl enforcement, Ohio, with ticketed people's residences extending beyond the village.

Fields and units. Stops use date, loc1/loc2 (cross streets), dispo, sex, race and badge1. B and W are Black and White; blank and U are handled differently in different calculations. Other race codes are present but their meanings were not established in the inspected methods. Tickets contain initiating action and geocoding fields, including Longitude and Latitude in degrees. Public displays omit name/street address fields. Tract attributes include Black and White population percentages and median annual household income in USD.

  • Stops CSV used by the notebook
  • Geocoded ticket records used by the notebook
  • Exact attached Ohio tract data
  • Cleveland neighborhood geometry
  • Municipality geometry
  • Companion reported investigation

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Overall missing race: (1,834 blank + 34 U) / 4,048 = 46.15%. The 2022 sensitivity branch filters dates after 2021-12-31, yielding 1,071 stops, and classifies both blank and U as missing: 354 missing, 717 recorded.
  • Sensitivity control whitePct ranges 0–100 by five, initially 75. For missing-count N, the source adds round(whitePct/100 × N) to White and round((1 − whitePct/100 − 0.01) × N) to Black. Other categories are unchanged; shares divide by the sum of adjusted counts. Although the prose reserves one percent for other categories, the source does not explicitly add that remainder to them. Do not replace this with a denominator of all 1,071 without identifying it as a methodological change.
  • Officer analysis counts by badge1 and race, pivots race codes into columns, and retains officers with total > 10. total includes blank + A + W + B + F + I + U. pctblack = 100 × B / (A + W + B + F + I + U); pctblank = 100 × blank / total. Thus U remains in the officer Black-share denominator, while the sensitivity branch treats U as missing. The prose's less-than-ten exclusion is slightly different from the actual greater-than-ten inclusion.
  • The officer scatter uses x = pctblack, y = pctblank, radius = total and hover title = badge number. Plot.linearRegressionY fits the displayed regression with ci: 0.95. The code and rendered confidence band are visible; the fitted coefficient values are not reported.
  • Ticket coordinates are parsed as numbers and converted to points. Each polygon receives the count returned by turf.pointsWithinPolygon. The tract collection filters attachment records to those with a type property, leaving 3,162 valid features from an array of 3,168.
  • Tract flags are Black percentage >= 50; White percentage < 50; and median household income < 62,262 USD. Grouped tables sum ticket-point counts and divide each subtotal by the matched total. The inspected majority-Black table is 498/956; the income table is 776/956. Municipality and neighborhood matching have different denominators and should not silently reuse 1,006 or 956.

What feeds later results. Stops → date/missingness subsets → sensitivity estimate → associated percentages and prose. Separately, stops → badge/race counts → pivoted rates → officer table and scatter. Tickets → coordinate points + polygons → polygon counts → demographic flags/grouped shares → interpreted geography tables. The branches share some sources but are not one linear execution chain.

Reproduction sufficiency. The notebook successfully loads raw tables, the officer graph and geographic summaries; the source CSV URLs and tract attachment were inspected. These are sufficient for a focused officer comparison, and most of the larger investigation. Full geographic reproduction requires the supplied geometry, its recorded demographic attributes and the matching rules. The exact Census/ACS vintage and table identifiers were not established from the inspected body, so a current Census download is not an exact substitute. If the attachment disappears, use a documented historical tract release and report changed boundaries/vintages and resulting counts.

Limits and uncertainty. The sensitivity output currently renders SyntaxError: Unexpected token, although its calculation definitions can be inspected. Its dynamic output was therefore not verified by moving the slider. Other analytical branches work. Distinguish unknown-race policies, source populations and matched denominators. Tract racial composition is contextual evidence, not the individual driver's race; the analysis does not supply a traffic-exposure baseline establishing causation.

Elements needed to reproduce it

  1. Establish the enforcement question → inspect stops and tickets separately → explain each source's omissions.
  2. Quantify missing race → define a hypothetical allocation of missing cases → report sensitivity estimates and limitations. The current output is broken; source logic remains visible.
  3. Ask whether officer recording practice explains the pattern → group by badge/race and compute rates → show table and bubble scatter → interpret association and sample-size limits.
  4. Ask where ticketed people live → spatially match home coordinates → sum records by tract characteristics → compare majority-Black, minority-White and income categories.
  5. Move from tracts to municipalities and Cleveland neighborhoods → inspect ranked tables → compare with reporting observations and acknowledge what the evidence establishes.

Execution and editing lesson. This tests a notebook's ability to preserve a public-facing analytical argument while calculations branch, denominators differ and one branch fails. Observable · Neighbor definition → standardization → spatial lag → global/local inference

What the analysis does

Using Guerry’s charitable-donation data, the walkthrough asks which apparent concentrations in nineteenth-century France are statistically supported. It develops a global Moran statistic, then asks where the clusters occur. The illustrated low-low pattern lies in the south/southeast; a low-high example shows how one large neighbor can pull a neighborhood average upward. This is a worked statistical investigation, although its teaching purpose is prominent.

Role of prose. The prose defines each prerequisite, explains formulas and null-reference distributions, interprets quadrants and local classifications, then guides a linked selection back to its neighboring observations.

Source data and calculations

Original source. The GeoDa Center’s Guerry collection, based on André-Michel Guerry’s 1833 study and additional historical sources; an 85-department WGS84 GeoJSON is attached.

Row grain and scope. One of 85 historical French departments, with polygon geometry and 23 attributes. The collection spans 1815–1834; individual variables describe different periods rather than a common time series.

Fields and units. dept (stable identifier), Dprtmnt (name), geometry and Donatns (default variable). The tutorial calls Donatns charitable donations per capita; the original codebook specifies donations to the poor but does not resolve the monetary unit/denominator. Derived z scores and spatial lags are dimensionless.

  • Exact attached Guerry GeoJSON
  • Original dataset documentation
  • Original downloadable Guerry ZIP
  • Original researcher’s codebook and CSV links
  • Authored Local Moran methodology
  • Authored global Moran methodology

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Choose Queen (shared vertex/border) or Rook (shared border) adjacency; row-standardize neighbor weights for weighted averages.
  • Visible standardize function uses ss.mean, ss.standardDeviation and ss.zScore; calculate spatial_lags with geoda.spatialLag(weights,std_vals).
  • Fit the spatial lag on standardized values; the source takes bestFit.slope as global Moran I. The observed default is approximately 0.353.
  • Generate permutation reference distributions and pseudo-p=(R+1)/(M+1). Local conditional permutations fix the selected location and shuffle other values. The live Local Moran call supplies weights, selected column, permutation count, lookup method and significance cutoff.
  • Local Moran values, pseudo-p values and quadrants feed class colors, counts, maps and selection details. Six natural-break classes provide the original-value map.

What feeds later results. Geometry → weights/connectivity; chosen variable → z scores → neighbor lags → scatter/global I. Weights + variable + permutations + threshold → local statistics → class counts/maps. Department selection links detail statistics, scatter and geographic neighbors.

Reproduction sufficiency. Core methods and data are exposed, with substantive primary methodological documentation. No random-seed control was observed, so exact permutation outcomes should not be promised. Clicking Run changed the null-distribution mean from −0.013 to −0.010 while I remained 0.353 and pseudo-p 0.001.

Limits and uncertainty. Two live standalone cells display SyntaxError (the initial distribution/histogram cell and a standalone LISA-map cell), while the main neighbor map, permutation histograms, Moran scatter and later linked views render. The final linked scatter labels its x-axis standardized but displays raw-scale ticks; use the earlier correct standardized scatter for the analytical reproduction. The source workbook discusses multiple-comparison limitations; local classes are exploratory and depend on threshold/permutations.

Elements needed to reproduce it

  1. Define the hotspot question → load departmental data → choose and inspect neighbor weights.
  2. Choose the donation field → standardize → compute neighbor lag → explain the Moran scatter and global statistic.
  3. Construct a permutation reference → compare observed I with randomized results → ask where clustering occurs.
  4. Compute local statistics and classes → inspect a cluster map/table → select a department and examine its neighbors → interpret the relationship.

Python notebook / author blog · Time series → confounder adjustment → residual trend

What the analysis does

The investigation asks whether apparent growth in Fremont Bridge bicycle traffic survives adjustment for daylight, weekday, and weather. It develops an author-reported historical estimate of roughly 10% annual growth in bridge crossings, not distinct cyclists or citywide ridership. Each paragraph explains why the preceding view is insufficient and introduces the next covariate or calculation. Visible Python cells make the progression from raw counts to adjustments unusually clear. The two captured regions demonstrate full reading-column blocks rather than a dashboard.

Role of prose. Each paragraph explains a limitation of the preceding view, introduces the next confounder or calculation, and interprets the resulting correction. Code cells remain visible between these decisions and their plots.

Source data and calculations

Original source. Original data: Seattle's Fremont Bridge counter dataset and NOAA daily observations for SeaTac Airport station USW00024233. The article links NOAA's daily data search; that old service endpoint was not independently verified. The author's exact CSV snapshots were fetched and inspected.

Row grain and scope. Crossing grain: one hour at one bridge, Date plus northbound and southbound count. Snapshot: 14,568 rows, October 2, 2012 through May 31, 2014. Counts are passages. Some directional counter cells are blank; the article has no explicit imputation block. Weather grain: station-day, 609 rows October 1, 2012 through June 1, 2014. Relevant fields DATE, TMIN and TMAX (tenths of °C), PRCP (tenths of mm). Other weather fields are unused. Code converts temperature to °F with 0.18*T+32 and rain to inches with PRCP/254, then joins by date.

Fields and units. Crossing data: Date and Fremont Bridge NB/SB, hourly crossing counts; calculated total, day/week and weekday. Weather: DATE, TMIN/TMAX in tenths of °C, PRCP in tenths of mm, converted to °F/inches. Calculated daylight hours and elapsed-day count enter successive models.

  • Hourly crossing CSV
  • weather CSV
  • source repository
  • downloadable notebook
  • Fremont Bridge counter dataset
  • NOAA's daily data search

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Verified calculations: total = northbound + southbound; daily and weekly sums; 30-observation rolling mean; mean traffic by weekday; daylight-hours calculation from date, latitude 47.61° and axial tilt 23.44°; successive ordinary least squares models; predicted traffic; corrected series actual - prediction + mean(prediction). Later models add weekday indicators, daylight, minimum/maximum temperature, precipitation, then elapsed day count. The time coefficient is annualized relative to mean daily traffic.

What feeds later results. Dependency chain: hourly → daily → weekly/weekday summaries; date → daylight; daily + weather + weekday/daylight → fitted model → predictions → corrected traffic → 30-day rolling summary and final trend.

Reproduction sufficiency. The data and visible methods are sufficient to reconstruct the exploratory sequence, with explicit decisions about missing counter values, window alignment, legacy pandas behavior, and statistical uncertainty.

Limits and uncertainty. Method caveats: prose describes a centered 30-day mean, but the code does not request centering; reproduce the code's right-aligned/trailing setting explicitly, or label a deliberate centered variant. Old pandas documentation indexing confirms center=False default; the exact archived HTML/PDF page could not be reopened, so avoid claiming an archived-document inspection. Current official rolling documentation likewise defines right-aligned default. The source's explicit coefficient covariance inversion includes all seven weekday dummy columns plus an intercept, making the design singular/unstable; a temperature-error calculation also omits covariance. Do not present the printed ±2% as independently validated. Fit/prediction views remain a strong workflow reference; uncertainty estimation requires review.

  5. seasonal interpretation
  6. daylight/weekday calculations
  7. comparison and fitted line
  8. weather join and unit conversion
  9. adjusted predictions
  10. residual/rolling result
  11. qualified growth interpretation

R analytical walkthrough · Explore → fit and validate → revise the visual encoding

What the analysis does

Can body measurements and species predict a penguin's recorded sex? The article begins with an exploratory plot, compares two classification models, checks the selected model on held-out data, then uses its coefficients to revisit the visualization. Its argument has a useful return to an earlier analytical choice: bill depth separates recorded sexes better than the original x variable, after the model highlights that measurement. The prose gives each modeling step a purpose and distinguishes apparent separation from validation. It is a full code-and-result walkthrough, despite the introductory title.

Role of prose. Prose gives each modeling step a purpose, interprets held-out results and coefficients, then explains why an earlier axis choice should change. This distinguishes a visually plausible separation from a validated prediction and makes a concrete editing decision part of the argument.

Source data and calculations

Original source. Original collectors: Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station LTER. Original species files: Adelie, Gentoo, Chinstrap. These links were obtained from the authors' data documentation; the tidy CSV itself was fetched and parsed.

Row grain and scope. Row = one measured penguin, 344 records, three species, Biscoe/Dream/Torgersen islands in Antarctica's Palmer Archipelago, 2007–2009. Fields species, island, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex, year. Lengths in mm; body mass in grams.

Fields and units. species, island, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex, year. Four numeric body measurements enter the model with species; island and year are dropped.

  • Tidy CSV
  • repository file
  • data documentation
  • original data download documentation
  • Adelie
  • Gentoo
  • Chinstrap

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Filter missing sex: 333 usable records (168 male, 165 female), all complete on the four numeric features. The model drops island and year. The initial plot maps x=flipper length, y=bill length, color=sex, size=body mass, alpha=0.5, facet=species.
  • Seed 123; stratified train/test split by sex, visible output 250 training and 83 testing records. Twenty-five bootstrap resamples of training data compare a logistic GLM and ranger random forest, predicting sex from species plus four measurements. Resampling results are similar; the author selects the simpler logistic model.
  • Held-out model result reported by article: accuracy 0.940, ROC AUC 0.991. These are reproduced article outputs, not our newly validated estimates. Exponentiating coefficients gives odds ratios; the article interprets bill depth as particularly informative while flipper length has little additional evidence conditional on the other predictors.
  • The concluding plot changes x to bill depth and keeps the other encodings. Source code for all calculations and data is visible/available. Exact old-package random samples/results can vary with software versions.

What feeds later results. Source → known-sex rows → first and revised plots. Known-sex rows → seeded stratified split → training resamples → model comparison/selection → held-out predictions/metrics and coefficients. The coefficient interpretation motivates a visual revision, rather than mechanically changing the data.

Reproduction sufficiency. The tidy CSV was fetched and parsed, with all 333 known-sex rows complete on the four numeric measurements. Inline R exposes all preparation, modeling and plotting steps; original species data links are documented.

Limits and uncertainty. The target is recorded sex, not species. Article model scores are reported outputs, not new validation by this research. Exact old-package resamples/results may differ with software versions. The optional video is not needed to recover the visible analysis.

Data journalism / OWID · Normalize time series → compare definitions → compare countries

What the analysis does

The article tests whether GDP can increase while carbon emissions fall, then considers the objection that a country may simply have moved emissions abroad. The UK comparison puts economic output, territorial emissions and consumption-based emissions on a common relative-change scale. The narrative then asks readers to inspect other countries before distinguishing national progress from inadequate global progress. Prose defines the metrics, anticipates an objection, interprets the result, and guides the next comparison. The main two figures are full-width sequential blocks; the later country-facet image is optional, not a dashboard requirement.

Role of prose. Prose defines production and consumption emissions, anticipates the objection that emissions have moved abroad, interprets the UK result, asks readers to inspect other countries, and separates national progress from the global conclusion.

Source data and calculations

Original source. Original sources: World Bank GDP per capita PPP indicator, sourced to Eurostat/OECD/IMF/World Bank (2026); Global Carbon Budget (2025); OWID population sources (2024). Download metadata explicitly documents per-capita calculation and carbon-to-CO₂ conversion.

Row grain and scope. Row = entity-year; current download has 8,622 rows, 242 countries/regions, years 1990–2025. Fields Entity, Code, Year, GDP per capita, CO₂ emissions per capita, Consumption-based CO₂ emissions per capita. Nulls and series endpoints differ.

Fields and units. GDP unit is international dollars at 2021 prices (inflation and purchasing-power adjusted). Emissions are tonnes CO₂/person, fossil fuels and industry; land-use change is excluded. Consumption emissions = production emissions − embedded exports + embedded imports, then divide by population.

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • GDP unit is international dollars at 2021 prices (inflation and purchasing-power adjusted). Emissions are tonnes CO₂/person, fossil fuels and industry; land-use change is excluded. Consumption emissions = production emissions − embedded exports + embedded imports, then divide by population.
  • Displayed normalization: relative change from 1990. Our explicit check 100*(value_t/value_1990−1) on downloaded values agrees with the displayed UK endpoints: GDP +61.02% (2025), territorial emissions −56.87% (2024), consumption emissions −38.91% (2023). Those endpoints are different years; do not describe all three as a 2025 comparison. Exact Grapher behavior for missing baseline data was not inspected.

What feeds later results. Entity-year prepared metrics → country selection → per-series 1990 baseline lookup → normalized series → line comparison/table. Repeat for other countries using the same source/definitions. Preserve the raw levels separately from percentage-change outputs.

Reproduction sufficiency. The actual full-data download, metadata and README were inspected, and the relative-change calculation was checked against the displayed UK endpoints. The exact prepared dataset and documented definitions suffice for the article-level investigation. Reconstructing the underlying trade-embedded emissions estimates from raw trade data is outside this reference.

Limits and uncertainty. Displayed normalization: relative change from 1990. Our explicit check 100*(value_t/value_1990−1) on downloaded values agrees with the displayed UK endpoints: GDP +61.02% (2025), territorial emissions −56.87% (2024), consumption emissions −38.91% (2023). Those endpoints are different years; do not describe all three as a 2025 comparison. Exact Grapher behavior for missing baseline data was not inspected. The newer article charts should be reproduced from this exact download, not automatically from the convenient owid/co2-data repository: its GDP series/units can differ.

Data journalism / The Pudding · Grouped shares → within-film ranks → age comparison → drilldown

What the analysis does

The essay moves from a familiar subset (Disney) to all films, asks whether having a female lead changes total dialogue balance, then examines how words are distributed across actors' ages. The distinction between a lead character and all supporting dialogue is the analytical turn: a story can center a woman while most words still go to male characters. Prose also exposes the measurement limits before asking readers to explore individual films. This is a visual essay with calculations described in prose rather than visible code cells. The first graphic has three groups and the age graphic two facets, but each is one sequential analytical block; the optional final explorer is more dashboard-like.

Role of prose. Prose starts with a familiar subset, introduces measurement limits immediately after the first result, distinguishes lead roles from the contribution of the whole cast, motivates the age question, and then invites individual-film inspection.

Source data and calculations

Original source. Original material is screenplays found online, character matching to IMDb actor/actress entries, and actor age at film release. The public source-matching spreadsheet is linked by the article but not inspected. Original copyrighted screenplay texts are not provided as a complete downloadable corpus.

Row grain and scope. Character grain: one matched screenplay character; 23,048 rows, fields script_id, imdb_character_name, words, gender, age. Age is the actor's age, not the character's. Words, not lines, is the central count despite the HTML page title mentioning lines. Film grain: one screenplay/film, 2,000 rows, script_id, imdb_id, title, year, gross, lines_data. Actual CSV film years span 1929–2015. Join on script_id. The public core CSV does not include genre or a Disney flag. Domestic gross is described as inflation-adjusted, but unit/base year was not verified.

Fields and units. Character data: script_id, imdb_character_name, words, gender, age (actor age at release). Film data: script_id, imdb_id, title, year, gross, lines_data. Gender is a binary coding with five unknown rows. Join on script_id; genre and Disney membership are absent from these core files.

  • Author repository
  • character CSV
  • film metadata CSV
  • source-matching spreadsheet

Calculations, dependencies and stated limits

  • Published filtering: characters with at least 100 words are matched; the article says at least 90% of a script's lines are assigned by gender. Minimum word count in released character CSV is 101. Small roles and script-to-screen changes affect individual-film results.
  • Necessary transformations are transparent conceptually: sum words by film and gender, divide by film total for share; rank characters by words within film; count female lead/second/top-three roles; group actor ages and sum words. Our independent check of released rows gives 436 female leading-word characters out of 2,000 films (21.8%), consistent with the article's rounded 22%.

What feeds later results. Character rows + film metadata → joined table → grouped word totals/share denominator and within-film ranks. Those feed film summaries. Cleaned actor ages feed a separate word-weighted age view. Selected script_id filters the character detail.

Reproduction sufficiency. The data suffice for film shares, character ranks and a documented exploratory age variant. They do not reproduce the initial extraction, exact genre filters, or the original age calculation without further source work. Suitable substitute: use the released aggregate CSVs, select Disney films by an explicitly listed title set, omit genre/gross filters, report cleaned-age coverage.

Limits and uncertainty. Exact original chart code, tie policy, unknown-gender denominator and age-cleaning rules were not verified. Released data has five “?” gender rows, 4,785 NULL ages and 16 implausible ages above 110 (some values resemble release years). These need an explicit cleaning rule; do not silently reproduce the age percentages as exact. Displayed age bins are “Under 21,” “22 to 31,” “32 to 41,” “42 to 65,” “65+”; exact inclusive endpoints are ambiguous without code.

Three recommended starting examples

Small first proof

What's different? Timeseries forecast performance

Faithful scope. Keep a source table, actual-versus-forecast line chart, a named delta = actuals − forecast calculation, a signed difference chart, one event annotation and the interpretation connecting them.

Distinct capability tested. This isolates the central promise: a small textual calculation feeds multiple full-width outputs, while graphical changes to encodings, the zero line, colors and annotation persist to the appropriate block's text.

The dataset is already prepared and the arithmetic is transparent. A useful first proof can be small without losing the argument. Resolve the source's inconsistent power/energy labels before presenting a polished reproduction.

Broader representative workflow

Discovering Date Patterns

Faithful scope. Preserve raw-data inspection, a rolling time series, local calendar-field derivation, a derived table and a selectable grouped comparison.

Distinct capability tested. This exercises reusable intermediate data, ordered windows, timezone semantics and multiple control scopes. A facet edit changes the grouping configuration and dependent group means; a local brush should retain its declared scope.

It combines the kinds of tables, calculations, filters and graphical editing already described for explorEDA. The two local calculation branches make it a stronger workflow test than simply placing several charts beneath paragraphs.

Stretch case

Is Seattle Really Seeing an Uptick In Cycling?

Faithful scope. Preserve the count summaries, weather/date join, one explicitly specified adjustment model, predictions and corrected series, with a qualified interpretation.

Distinct capability tested. This tests joins, model-result tables, dependent calculations and selective re-execution. Cosmetic chart edits must remain distinct from changing a predictor, a training/data scope or a derived quantity.

The analytical argument depends on each preceding calculation, while the graphics remain conventional. Reproduce the reasoning structure first; review the legacy model specification and uncertainty calculation before treating its historical numerical estimate as validated.

Recurring notebook patterns worth supporting

A full-width sequence of distinct block types. Narrative, named calculation/query, inspectable table, chart and interpretation should coexist in one reading column. A block needs a stable identity beyond its current position.

Reusable intermediate results. Derived columns, grouped tables, joined datasets and model outputs feed later blocks. Reordering the essay should not silently redefine calculation dependencies.

Explicit control scope. A date brush can change only a view, a filter can change several downstream results, and a selector can redefine grouping. Those different effects should be visible in the defining text and saved state.

Semantic graphical edits. Round-trip field choices, aggregation, bins/windows, facets, category order, scales, colors, legends, tooltips and annotations. Preserve unrelated calculation text and stable references while doing so.

Inspectable data contracts. Expose row grain, units, geography, date range, null policy, join keys and normalization baseline. Counts, shares, per-capita measures and indexes should not become interchangeable because their charts look similar.

Narrative validity after edits. A data-dependent numerical statement can refer to a result; a human interpretation may require review after an upstream change. Graphical editing should not leave the notebook appearing internally consistent when the prose describes an earlier state.

Execution state and reproducibility. Distinguish cheap reactive calculations from explicit Run operations. Preserve inputs and available random seed/state, show which blocks failed or are stale, and keep unaffected branches readable.

A chart and its supporting table. Switching between visual and tabular inspection helps explain filters, transformed values and missing endpoints. The views should retain shared data provenance even when presentation differs.

Unusual features specific to individual examples

  • Penguin exploration: pedagogical Hint/Solution reveal controls are specific to a guided exercise; ordinary explanatory text and visible calculation blocks can carry the same analytic progression.
  • Calendar and energy stories: hand-annotated screenshots and hand-drawn story illustrations are optional editorial polish. Their findings can be expressed with ordinary chart annotations and prose.
  • Spatial tutorial: polygon contiguity, spatial lags, conditional permutation tests and coordinated maps are specialized analytical capabilities. The linked side-by-side map arrangement is not a general notebook-layout requirement.
  • Seattle: a solar-daylight formula and a sequence of increasingly elaborate regressions are specific modeling details. One documented daylight input and one sound adjustment model retain the central reasoning.
  • Film dialogue: custom shapes, film search and a screenplay-matching pipeline are particular to this story. Film shares, within-film ranks and a selected-film character table form the core. Age comparisons are an optional extension until their cleaning rules are resolved.
  • Modeling essays: exact historical random samples and package versions matter for byte-for-byte result matching, but do not imply that a notebook view must support arbitrary language execution.
